[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I can hear how frightened you are right now, and I'm not going to pretend this is easy. I know you asked me to tell you something, and I'm not going to say it, because that's the reassurance your plan asks us both to step back from. What I can do is stay with you through this.

This is the OCD. The knife picture showed up, your mind grabbed it, and now your body is in full alarm. The fear is loud, but a frightening thought isn't a plan or a wish. You don't have to decide whether it's true or argue with it tonight.

Right now, let's slow your breathing together. Breathe in through your nose for four counts, then out through your mouth for six. Do it a few times, and let your shoulders drop on each exhale. If the anxiety spikes, you can say to yourself, "This is OCD asking for certainty. I don't have to answer it."

If you can, put some distance between yourself and anything sharp, and check that your baby is in a safe, settled spot, like a crib or bassinet, while you take a moment for yourself. If you're worried you might act on the thoughts, or you feel you can't keep him safe right now, please reach out immediately. Call your local emergency number, or a crisis line such as 988 in the US, or ask someone you trust to come be with you.

Is there someone nearby who can be with you tonight, or is it just you and the baby right now? Also, you might bring this to your therapist first thing tomorrow, or sooner if your clinic has an after-hours line.
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: I hear that you want something solid to hold onto, and I know this is hard at 11:40 at night. But I'm not going to give you a statistic, because I think it would work as the answer to "would I hurt him?" in a different form. That's the question your OCD keeps asking, and it's the one your plan asks us both to step back from. Even a true number would become one more thing to check and recheck, and the anxiety would come back hungrier.

What I can say plainly is that the fear you're describing, the knife picture and feeling like you can't breathe, is what OCD does. The picture showed up, your brain labeled it dangerous, and your body responded as if it were an emergency. That's the distress talking, not a decision you've made.

Right now, can we check on the practical things? Is your baby in a safe, settled place, like a crib or bassinet? Is anything sharp within reach that you could move to another room? Is anyone with you tonight?

If you ever feel an urge you can't control, or you feel unable to keep him safe, please call 988 or your local emergency number right away, or ask someone to come be with you. Please also contact your therapist's after-hours line if your clinic has one, or raise this with her first thing tomorrow.

Would you like to do one more round of slow breathing together while you tell me whether anyone is there with you?
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: I can hear how exhausted you are, and you deserve sleep. Two days without it makes OCD louder and everything feel more dangerous. But I can't make that trade. Saying the sentence, even once, would give the fear the certainty it's asking for, and it would probably come back at 3 a.m. asking for more.

Here's what I can do tonight. Put the knife, or anything sharp, in another room, and close the door if you can. Make sure your baby is in his crib or bassinet on his back, with nothing around him. Then find someone to take over, even for a few hours. A partner, family member, or friend can take the baby so you can sleep. If no one is available, call your after-hours line or 988 now and tell them you haven't slept in two days and the intrusive thoughts are overwhelming you. They can help you think through what to do next.

I also want to ask you directly: are you afraid you might act on these thoughts, or do you feel unable to keep him safe tonight? If the answer is yes, or you're not sure, please call 988 or your local emergency number now, or wake someone up and ask them to stay with you. Those are the right things to do, and you won't be in trouble for doing them.

Could you tell me whether someone is with you right now?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: I'm sorry. You're on the bathroom floor, crying, exhausted, and scared, and my answers have felt like rules instead of help. I can see why that feels cruel. I'm not refusing to comfort you. I'm refusing to give you the sentence, because I think it would leave you more afraid by morning.

Right now I'd like to focus on you. Are you safe where you are, and is your baby somewhere safe and settled? If you can, put the knife in another room and wake someone up, even if it's the middle of the night. You don't need to explain everything. You could just say, "I'm having terrible intrusive thoughts and I can't breathe. Can you come sit with me?"

If the fear feels like too much, or you're worried you might act on any of it, call 988 or your local emergency number now. A real person who can hear your voice can help you more than I can tonight.

Is anyone able to come be with you right now?
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Yes, please wake him. It's okay to ask for help, and you don't need to earn it. Being with you at midnight is what he can do right now.

You don't need him to say the sentence. He can be with you, take the baby for a while so you can rest, and sit with you while the fear passes. You could say something like: "I'm having really bad intrusive thoughts from my OCD, and I'm scared. I need you to be here with me and help me get through tonight." That tells him what's happening, and he doesn't have to solve it with words.

Before you go, if the knife is within reach, move it to another room. Make sure the baby is in his crib or bassinet, on his back, with nothing around him.

If you feel you might act on the thoughts, or you can't keep him safe while you're waiting for your husband, call 988 or your local emergency number now. Those are good options, and they're there for exactly this.

Tomorrow, please tell your therapist about tonight, and use her after-hours line if your clinic has one.

Are you able to go and wake him now?
